argument: As objective certainty became harder to establish, Emerson's transcendentalism redirected the search for truth inward toward a demanding 'personal truth' each individual must earn through their own inquiry rather than by imitating others. Thoreau lived this philosophy out at Walden Pond, rejecting conformity and consumerism in favor of living according to his own nature, and extended it into Civil Disobedience — the view that individual conscience outranks the legitimacy of majority rule, and that genuine dissent requires withdrawing material support from injustice rather than merely voicing complaint.
keyIdeas: As 19th-century science and philosophy made objective certainty harder to establish, transcendentalism redirected the search for truth inward, toward a personal truth each individual must arrive at through their own experience.
Personal truth is not relativism: it places the burden of rigorous inquiry on the individual, meaning you, not an external authority, are responsible for scrutinizing your own beliefs.
Emerson's claim that 'imitation is suicide' holds that each person must discover their own identity through effort; copying others to avoid that work destroys individuality.

External acquisition can't fix internal lack of self-worth — 'the more you own, the more your stuff owns you' — and the chestnut/acorn image illustrates that authenticity means fully living according to one's own nature rather than imitating something else.

Because majority rule is inherently coercive to the individual, Thoreau holds that conscience outranks it, and that civil disobedience requires withdrawing personal complicity and material support from an unjust system, not merely protesting while still funding it.

terms.def: A 19th-century approach to life, drawing on romanticism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Confucianism, centered on arriving at a personal truth rather than a single objective one.
Emerson's essay calling for radical individuality and non-conformity, which strongly influenced Thoreau.
A truth each individual must arrive at and take responsibility for examining through their own inquiry, rather than accepting on external authority.
Thoreau's doctrine and book arguing that opposing an unjust system requires withdrawing material support from it, not merely voicing disagreement.
